reading.title: 14.1.1 Obtaining an Address with &
paragraphs: The address-of operator & obtains a pointer to an object, as in int* selected = &reading;. The pointed-to type determines what object can be accessed through the pointer. The pointer itself is a separate object that can be copied or changed to refer elsewhere.

An address is meaningful within an execution environment, not a durable identifier for storage or a network protocol. Processes have their own address spaces, and allocation can reuse addresses after objects die. Do not write pointer values to a file and expect them to identify the same objects after restart. Use stable logical identifiers when identity must survive beyond one object’s lifetime.

The address-of operator & obtains a pointer to an existing object in the ordinary cases used here. In int* selected = &reading;, selected is a pointer object and reading is an integer object. The pointer stores an access value that identifies the target; it is not the target integer itself.

This explains why changing the pointer and changing the target are different operations. Assigning another valid address to selected changes which object it observes. Assigning through *selected changes the observed integer. A diagram should show both objects rather than drawing one box labeled “pointer/value.”

An address printed during a run is implementation and execution context, not a stable identifier for a record. Address-space layout, allocation, and object lifetimes can change between runs. Do not store a printed address in a file and expect it to identify the same object in a later process.

Declare one pointer per line when the distinction matters. In a declaration containing several names, the * syntax can make it easy to misread which names are pointers. Clear declarations are cheaper than debugging an incorrect type assumption.

The ampersand also appears in reference declarations, but its role differs by context. int& alias declares a reference type; &reading is an expression obtaining an address. Read the grammatical context before deciding what the symbol means. C++ reuses several symbols across declarations and expressions, so punctuation alone is not a sufficient mental model.

topics.chapterTitle: Working Directly with Memory Through Pointers
topics.title: 14.2.1 Initializing Pointers with nullptr
topics.summary: nullptr represents a null pointer value and communicates absence more clearly than an integer zero used for that purpose. Initialize optional pointers explicitly so that the absence state is defined. A pointer’s nullability belongs in the interface contract: can the caller omit the object, and what does the function do when it is absent?

Choose the representation that matches the domain rather than using pointers for every missing value.

blocks.text: Optionality belongs in the interface. A function accepting a pointer may permit null to mean “no result,” or it may require a nonnull pointer. The type alone does not specify every precondition, so document the convention. A reference is often appropriate when a valid existing object is required and absence would make no sense.

If null might mean missing record, invalid index, allocation failure, or expired data, callers cannot distinguish those outcomes without another channel. For the small selection example, null means that no in-range element was selected. More expressive error types are introduced in Book II.

topics.title: 14.2.2 Checking Pointer Validity Before Dereferencing
topics.summary: An if (pointer != nullptr) check establishes only that the pointer is not null. It cannot prove that the object is still alive. Correct pointer use depends on a design that bounds the pointer’s lifetime relative to the owner’s lifetime and prevents invalidation while access is in progress.

blocks.text: An if (pointer != nullptr) check establishes only that the pointer is not null. It cannot prove that the object is still alive. Correct pointer use depends on a design that bounds the pointer’s lifetime relative to the owner’s lifetime and prevents invalidation while access is in progress.
rich: An

check establishes only that the pointer is not null. It cannot prove that the object is still alive. Correct pointer use depends on a design that bounds the pointer’s lifetime relative to the owner’s lifetime and prevents invalidation while access is in progress.

blocks.text: For a pointer into a local array used within the same block, the relationship is straightforward. For a pointer stored in a long-lived object or passed between threads, it is not. Document whether a callee retains the pointer, whether a container may reallocate, and whether another thread can destroy the object. Prefer interfaces that make those relationships difficult to violate.

Prefer interfaces that make those relationships difficult to violate.

blocks.text: A null check answers one question: does this pointer contain the null value? It does not prove that a nonnull pointer refers to live, correctly typed, accessible storage. A pointer can remain nonnull after its object is destroyed, after a vector reallocates, or after it moves outside the permitted array range.

blocks.text: The validity argument therefore has several parts. The pointer must originate from an appropriate object or interface. The object must still be alive. The operation must stay within the permitted bounds. The access type and constness must be suitable. In this introductory example, those conditions follow from selecting an element of a known local array and avoiding structural mutation.

Forming an out-of-range pointer first and checking afterward can already violate the pointer-arithmetic rules. The guard must protect the operation, not merely the later dereference.

If the access must persist, the interface needs a stronger ownership or stable-identity design than a casual local nonnull check.

topics.summary: Why is nonnull insufficient? A nonnull value can still refer to expired, invalidated, out-of-range, or unsuitable storage. Nullness is only one part of validity.

cards.question: Why is nonnull insufficient?
cards.answer: A nonnull value can still refer to expired, invalidated, out-of-range, or unsuitable storage. Nullness is only one part of validity.

cards.question: Why may an end pointer exist without being dereferenced?
cards.answer: It represents the boundary of a permitted half-open range, not an additional element.

cards.question: Why does assigning null not repair every alias?
cards.answer: It changes one pointer object. Other copies of the old pointer value remain unchanged.

cards.question: Why distinguish the pointer from its target?
cards.answer: Operations can modify either one. Confusing them creates defects that may remain memory-safe while changing the wrong state.
